title: Concurrency, cancellation and async progress
summary: Trace progress, cancellation, admission and execution context under the actual runtime. Independently synthesized concurrency entrypoint concepts supplement operation-specific references; async syntax and Arc alone do not establish thread safety.

checks.question: Can this lock scope prevent another operation needed for progress, or block a runtime worker unacceptably?
checks.applicability: Lock ordering changes, critical sections, awaits while holding guards, and shared-state access.
valid_counterexamples: A short uncontended synchronous critical section can appropriately use std::sync::Mutex.
An async mutex guard may intentionally span an await for an I/O resource.
evidence_needed: Concrete lock type and guard scope.
Potentially conflicting paths and acquisition order.
Runtime topology and the awaited operation's dependencies.
not_a_rule: Mutex is not always wrong in async code.
Holding any lock across any await is not universally incorrect.
try_lock without a progress strategy can replace deadlock with starvation or busy waiting.

checks.question: If this future is dropped at a suspension point, is state left consistent and is transferred work accounted for?
checks.applicability: select!, timeouts, shutdown, task abort, multi-step state transitions, and queued work.
valid_counterexamples: The operation explicitly permits partial progress and exposes how to resume.
A task owns completion independently and the caller only stops waiting.
evidence_needed: Library guarantees for the specific operation.
State before cancellation and any compensating action.
not_a_rule: Timeout does not necessarily roll back work.
Cancellation safety must be evaluated per operation, not per async function label.

checks.question: Can the changed spawning or queueing behavior accumulate more work than the system can service?
checks.applicability: Unbounded channels, per-request spawning, fan-out, blocking work, and overload handling.
valid_counterexamples: An explicit admission controller limits concurrency upstream.
evidence_needed: Arrival rate or input bound and service capacity.
not_a_rule: Every channel need not have the same capacity.
spawn_blocking is not unlimited admission control.
Not all application state must be Sync; requirements depend on actual use and framework bounds.

checks.question: Does the chosen task or thread boundary support the captured values and keep long-running work from starving unrelated operations?
checks.applicability: Changing executors, moving code into spawned futures, adding blocking calls to async paths, or replacing Rc with Arc.
valid_counterexamples: A local executor intentionally keeps non-Send state on one thread.
A bounded amount of CPU work runs directly in a future without harming its latency budget.
A dedicated worker handles blocking I/O without occupying runtime workers.
evidence_needed: Executor version, worker topology and spawn API requirements.
Captured types, values retained across suspension and required Send/Sync bounds.
Duration and frequency of blocking or CPU work, plus worker admission limits.
not_a_rule: Arc<T> has thread-transfer and sharing bounds on T; it does not make arbitrary contents thread-safe.
Async code can block and is not automatically Send.
I/O may be served by synchronous threads; CPU work may be orchestrated by async code.
